open_obligations: Check that the nip losses are indeed not zero-sum in the sense Chen et al. intend.
Check which training method Hammond and Adam-Day use for nip; the cited passage does not state it.
Check whether Chen et al.'s oracle-based regret results apply to these games.
Check whether Hammond and Adam-Day run nip empirically, since Chen et al. call for an empirical study and the cited passage gives only the definition.

Check whether nip is instantiated as a language game with language-model provers and verifiers; the cited passage defines an abstract one-prover, one-verifier PVG and does not mention language or debate.
out.other_title: Experiments limited to zero-sum debate games
out.rationale: Chen et al. limit their experiments to zero-sum games and call the empirical study of general-sum language games an interesting future direction. Hammond and Adam-Day define nip with the prover's loss as worst-case positive-instance loss minus worst-case negative-instance loss and the verifier's loss as their sum, so the game is not zero-sum. The cited nip passage gives only a definition, with no experiment and no mention of language, so it does not answer Chen et al.'s call, and Chen et al.'s limitation does not bear on the definition; neither bears on the other's claim.
out.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: games that are not zero-sum, namely Chen et al.'s call for empirical study of general-sum language games beyond their zero-sum experiments, and nip, a prover-verifier game with one prover and one verifier whose losses are not zero-sum

text: The authors define the nip protocol as a prover-verifier game with one prover and one verifier exchanging alternating messages, where the prover's loss is the worst-case loss on positive instances minus the worst-case loss on negative instances and the verifier's loss is their sum. They state it is straightforward to show this corresponds closely to the notion of an interactive proof.
title: nip protocol: one prover and one verifier with worst-case losses
